issues.legal_issue: Rights granted by a former sovereign cannot be enforced against a successor sovereign unless the successor sovereign has recognized them.
material_facts: A former ruler granted forest rights to holders of specified tenures, who later contracted with the claimants to cut and remove timber.
Forest officials permitted some cutting only temporarily, subject to undertakings that the claimants would abide by the government’s eventual decision.
The successor government did not recognize the forest rights and ultimately rejected them.
issues.conclusion: The forest rights could not be enforced against the successor government. The temporary permissions given by subordinate forest officials did not recognize the rights or waive the government’s position.
issues.legal_principle: Under the rule applied in Secretary of State in Council for India v. Kamachee Boye Sahiba, Secretary of State v. Bai Rajbai, Vajesinghji Joravarsingji v. Secretary of State for India, Secretary of State v. Sardar Rustam Khan, and Asrar Ahmed v. Durgah Committee, rights derived from a former sovereign are enforceable against the successor only if the successor recognizes them expressly or by implication. The Court applied that rule consistently with M/s. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, State of Saurashtra v. Memon Haji Ismail Haji, Jagan Nath Agarwala v. State of Orissa, State of Saurashtra v. Jamadar Mohamed Abdulla, and Promod Chandra Deb v. State of Orissa, and disapproved the contrary approach in Virendra Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh. Recognition must be attributable to the successor sovereign; conditional action by subordinate officers does not suffice.

predicates.civil_claim_to_enforce_former_sovereign_: A claimant brought a civil proceeding seeking to enforce against a successor government a right granted by a former sovereign.
predicates.successor_did_not_recognize_grant: The successor government did not expressly or impliedly recognize the claimed right.
predicates.officials_allowed_work_only_conditionall: Subordinate officials allowed the claimant to work the resource temporarily, subject to the government’s later decision and an undertaking to abide by it.

issues.definition: When a civil claim seeks to enforce a former sovereign’s grant, the successor did not recognize it, and officials allowed work only conditionally, the grant is not enforceable against the successor.

issues.legal_issue: A person cannot enforce a covered covenant in a pre-Constitution agreement with a former ruler in a municipal court.
material_facts: A government letter accompanying a merger arrangement guaranteed that certain earlier orders and actions of the former ruler would not be questioned, subject to stated qualifications.
The claimants were not parties to the merger arrangement or the letter, but relied on the letter to argue that the successor government had relinquished its ability to reject the forest grant.
issues.conclusion: The claimants could not enforce the covenant in the municipal courts; if they had been parties to the agreement, the constitutional bar would have prevented that claim as well.
issues.legal_principle: Article 363 of the Constitution bars municipal courts from adjudicating disputes arising from covered agreements with former rulers. Under Maharaj Umeg Singh v. State of Bombay, a person who is not a party to such an agreement cannot enforce its covenants; a party is barred by Article 363. The agreement cannot independently establish recognition or waiver where the covenant itself is not enforceable in court.

predicates.municipal_claim_seeks_enforcement_of_cov: A claimant brought a municipal-court proceeding seeking to enforce a covenant in a pre-Constitution agreement with a former ruler.

issues.definition: If a municipal-court claim seeks enforcement of a covered pre-Constitution agreement with a former ruler, the covenant is not enforceable in that court.

issues.legal_issue: Constitutional protections against deprivation of property do not protect an unrecognized claim against the successor sovereign.
material_facts: The claimant’s asserted forest right came from a grant by the former ruler.
The successor government had not recognized that right before the constitutional protections were invoked.

The State succession affecting the inhabitants had occurred before the Constitution came into force; the later constitutional change did not itself create a property right enforceable against the successor.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could not rely on section 299(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, or Article 31 of the Constitution to enforce the unrecognized grant against the successor government.
issues.legal_principle: Section 299(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, and Article 31 of the Constitution protect an existing right to property; they do not create a right that is not enforceable against the State. As applied in State of Saurashtra v. Jamadar Mohamed Abdulla and Promod Chandra Deb v. State of Orissa, recognition by the successor is necessary before a former ruler’s grant can be enforced against it. The succession in respect of the former State’s inhabitants had already occurred; the Constitution did not initiate a new succession or convert an unrecognized claim into a protected property right.

predicates.claim_against_successor_state: A claimant sought to enforce a property claim against the State that succeeded the former sovereign.
predicates.property_claim_arose_under_former_sovere: The asserted property interest originated in a grant or other act of the former sovereign.
predicates.successor_had_not_recognized_claim: The successor State had not recognized the asserted interest.

issues.definition: When a property claim against a successor State originated under a former sovereign and the successor had not recognized it, constitutional property protection does not make the claim enforceable.

issues.legal_issue: An order granting forest benefits is not a law continued in force when it does not lay down a binding rule of conduct.
material_facts: The ruler’s order granted forest rights to holders of specified categories of village tenures after considering their complaints.
The order did not prescribe a binding rule of conduct and was in substance a grant of rights; its direction that forest management follow State policy did not alter that character.
The claimants argued that the order continued as law and could not be displaced by executive action.
issues.conclusion: The order was a grant, not a law continued in force; the claimants could not rely on its status as law to defeat the successor government’s executive action.
issues.legal_principle: A legislative act must lay down a binding rule of conduct. The distinction between legislative and executive action remains relevant even when an absolute ruler exercises both powers. The Court applied Articles 366(10) and 372 of the Constitution and clause 4 of the Administration of the Indian States Order, 1948. It distinguished Madhorao Phalke v. State of Madhya Bharat and Ameer-un-Nissa Begum v. Mahboob Begum, and relied on Maharaja Shree Umaid Mills Ltd. v. Union of India and Bengal Nagpur Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Board of Revenue, Madhya Pradesh.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_to_enforce_former_ruler: A claimant sought to enforce an order of a former ruler on the basis that it remained in force as law.
predicates.order_grants_specific_benefits: The order conferred specified benefits or rights on a defined group of recipients.
predicates.order_does_not_lay_down_binding_rule_of_: The order did not prescribe a binding rule governing conduct.

issues.definition: If a proceeding seeks to enforce a former ruler’s order as continuing law, the order grants specified benefits, and it does not lay down a binding rule of conduct, the order is not law continued in force.
